# On International Book Day, read without limits and with all your senses.

**Every April 23rd, since 1988, UNESCO has promoted the celebration of International Book and Copyright Day. EAFIT joins in this celebration with an invitation to reflect on access to reading and knowledge for people with disabilities.**

**Despite technological advances in electronic devices that facilitate reading for people with visual disabilities, there are still major challenges in digital literacy, production of books in braille and diversification of topics with accessible reading.**

- [Start](https://www.eafit.edu.co/)
- [News](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias)
- [Our Talent Community](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/nuestra-comunidad-de-talento)
- On International Book Day, Read Without Limits and With All Your Senses

![Image: On International Book Day, read without limits and with all your senses](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/c7ffd090-1002-4d14-8e80-06322ac514df/web/Libro-leer.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=823&h=450&itok=jMd6Hh30)

This site provides information on the services and resources available at the EAFIT Library to support the research and cultural processes of different populations.

Traveling to other worlds, fostering creativity, and expanding knowledge are just some of the possibilities that reading offers, but what happens when books cannot be read due to language or other barriers, limiting their enjoyment to a segment of society? This generates segregation and isolation, a common situation for people with disabilities.

On International Book and Copyright Day, celebrated every April 23rd around the world, it is fitting to reflect on the progress and challenges related to book accessibility. Patricia Ospina Ospina, head of the [Luis Echavarría Villegas Library and Cultural Center at EAFIT University](http://portalqa.omega.eafit.edu.co/centro-cultural-biblioteca-luis-echavarria-villegas) , highlights the significant advancement in the digitization of books with special features for people with visual and hearing impairments. "These texts allow software to read them aloud, adjusting the font size, contrast, and colors according to individual needs," she explains.

The increase in digital subscription-based platforms offering e-books and audiobooks, the development of devices such as scanners and braille tablets, as well as the establishment of accessibility standards, have motivated publishers to include new provisions and be more flexible, Patricia adds.

“These laws help ensure that, if a person with a disability requires a voice reader, the publisher removes the security protection from the document,” he says, although he points out that the challenge of diversifying the topics remains, where, incidentally, literature has a greater advantage in terms of accessibility than academic texts.

Likewise, the arrival of these digital tools implies processes of literacy, appropriation and visibility, this being a front that still needs to be covered and in which libraries play a fundamental role so that information reaches the users who need it most and can make beneficial use of it.

Regarding these digitization processes, Esteban Duperly Posada, head of EAFIT Publishing, argues that while audiobooks address some access issues, they eliminate a central component of the reading experience: the physical contact with paper. He also highlights the complexity and scarcity of Braille book production, as well as the need to broaden our perspective to include other dimensions of disability.

“Do bookstores and libraries have accessible shelves for people of short stature, wheelchair users, or those with reduced mobility? That’s a great question. Also, is the staff at these establishments trained to assist people who use sign language? That opens up a wide range of possibilities because, in general, the world isn’t designed for people with disabilities. And, of course, the book world is no exception,” says Esteban.

###### Library for everyone

Since 2015, the EAFIT Library has intensified its efforts to provide accessible information resources and services for people with disabilities. This aligns with its mission to democratize knowledge, bringing science and culture closer to students, faculty, and the general public.

In this regard, the University has bibliographic databases containing collections of literary, academic, and scientific texts in audio formats, such as Libby, Jove, Naxos, Project Gutenberg, O'Reilly, Digitalia, and Legis. Of a total of 153,000 ebooks, approximately 138,000 are available for audio, representing 90% of the collection.

In addition to the accessible spaces marked in Braille, the Library has magnifying glasses to facilitate the reading of printed material, high-contrast keyboards that allow the use of computers and the internet, software such as Magnification Magic and Jaws to listen to information or increase the size of the letters, a scanner service to read documents and books in Spanish, French, German and English, and a Braille Note Touch digital tablet that allows people with some type of visual impairment to perform common tasks.

Patricia points out that the library team already has people trained in sign language at a basic level, in order to guide and assist those who require it; however, she believes that the challenge is "to understand each of the disabilities in order to better adapt our services, technologies, literacy and education to the community in general," she states.
